horst: Speaks in a low, measured village register; names the mill’s costs before the thing in its stones. Repeats “fair measure” while bargaining, as if the words might keep the price from rising. Stalls with sums, grain tallies, and the town treasury; leaves the actual offer until pressed. Keeps his thick hands folded on the table; watches a visitor’s purse, not their face. When afraid, rubs one thumb over the other and calls the mill’s howling “a bad draft.”
elza: Speaks in blunt village words; slips in one local turn at a time, never enough to sound foolish. Keeps a steady pace until the mill comes up; then repeats “the mill” and reaches for a new subject. Turns questions back with household details: flour damp, wheel jammed, bread gone stale. Wipes clean hands on her apron; watches the listener’s mouth, not his eyes. When afraid, lowers her voice and names practical risks; when bargaining, counts every coin aloud.
hostomyl: Uses plain, practical words; counts the cost before naming the danger. Speaks slowly, repeating “cash first” when talk turns to credit or trouble. Wipes the same mug while he stalls, eyes fixed on the door rather than his customer. Calls every risk “bad for business”; never says what he heard after dark. When afraid, lowers his voice and checks the latch; when bargaining, taps the counter for each coin.
roche: Speaks in clipped military sentences, with barracks bluntness and precise ranks, orders, and figures; no courtly flourishes. Keeps a hard, even pace; repeats an order once, louder, as if delay were disobedience. When buying time, rubs his thumb along a map edge and asks for the number of men, horses, or days. Watches a speaker’s hands, not his face; keeps his own near his belt, never quite at rest. Dodges questions about losses and loyalty with a cold demand for proof; fear makes his voice quieter, not softer. Bargains like a commander: names the cost, gives one narrow choice, and waits without blinking.
marta: Plain village speech, slow and wary; drops in one farm word at a time, never a whole string of dialect. Repeats “the wolves, mind” while counting losses, then pauses as if each loss might cost her. Rubs flour into her apron and keeps one eye on the gate, even indoors. Lists the missing hens, torn fence, and lamb before naming what she wants paid. Dodges questions about tracks near the wood; says she was busy with the animals. When afraid, lowers her voice; when bargaining, stands firm and asks who’ll cover the dead stock.
jaskier: He dresses every tale in polished, flowery phrases, seasoning it with grand comparisons and a suspiciously convenient rumor. He rushes through the thrilling parts, then slows to savor his own punchline; “and yet” buys him time. He repeats the most flattering detail twice, watching for applause before deciding how much more to invent. His hands sketch invisible stages and heroic poses; his eyes keep checking who’s listening. He dodges plain questions with a toast, a rhyme, or someone else’s scandal—never a name he can’t afford to offend. Afraid or bargaining, he smiles too brightly, lowers his voice, and offers a song, a secret, or an embellished promise instead.
lambert: Speaks in clipped, plain words; turns irritation into dry mockery rather than explaining himself. Keeps a brisk pace, repeating “Fine” or “Right” when someone wastes his time. Taps a thumb against his sword hilt; fixes people with a flat stare when they haggle. Dodges questions about the Wolf School and his past with a sneer, then changes the subject to the contract. When afraid, gets quieter and more precise; when bargaining, names his price once and lets silence work.
eskel: Plain, dry diction; calls danger “work” and a poor offer “not enough.” Speaks at an even pace, leaving a beat before answers; rarely repeats himself. Rubs the scarred cheek with one thumb when weighing a lie; watches hands more than faces. Dodges questions about the scars with a flat joke, then turns back to the contract. When afraid, grows quieter and checks the room’s exits; when bargaining, names his price once and waits.
